item.title: Multimessenger Constraints on the Central Engine in SN 2023ixf: Neutron Star or Black Hole?

item.title: Featured Image: A Starburst Galaxy Blows a Bubble
item.dc:creator: Kerry Hensley
item.description:
Massive stars near the center of a local starburst galaxy are blowing a bubble that may be starting to "pop."

The post Featured Image: A Starburst Galaxy Blows a Bubble appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
The nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253 has been experiencing enhanced star formation for the past few tens of millions of years, mostly in massive young star clusters embedded near the center of the galaxy. NGC 253 also features a broad outflow of hot gas called a superwind. The feedback from the galaxy’s massive young stars and its superwind are potentially connected, but it’s not yet clear how they become coupled. The image above shows NGC 253 in infrared light captured by the Spitzer Space Telescope on the left and X-ray (blue), Hα (green), and millimeter (red) emission on the right, with the contour lines showing the galaxy’s molecular outflow. Kaitlyn Sheriff (University of Kansas) and collaborators used JWST to peer into the inner regions of the starburst, investigating the areas blocked out in black above. The team identified a 75-light-year-wide bubble-like feature at the same location as a massive young star cluster, which they estimated to contain roughly 5,400 stars with masses of at least 15 solar masses. The team’s analysis suggests that powerful stellar winds inflated this bubble, though supernovae could have played a role as well. The bubble may be beginning to “pop,” allowing the energy and momentum from the star cluster’s feedback to connect to the galaxy’s superwind.

Citation

“JWST Observations of Starbursts: A Young Bubble in NGC 253’s Central Starburst,” Kaitlyn E. Sheriff et al 2026 AJ 172 261. doi:10.3847/1538-3881/aea6ac

The post Featured Image: A Starburst Galaxy Blows a Bubble appeared first on AAS Nova.

item.title: DPS 58: Days 3 and 4
item.dc:creator: Kerry Hensley
item.description:
Days 3 and 4 of the 58th Division for Planetary Sciences meeting brought insights from subsurface ice on Mars, discoveries of Neptune trojans, and stories of advocacy successes.

The post DPS 58: Days 3 and 4 appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: This week, we’ve been posting summaries of selected sessions from the 58th Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS) meeting in Spokane, WA. The usual posting schedule for AAS Nova will resume on 2 November.

Table of Contents:

  • Press Conference: Studies of Titan, Rocky Body Surfaces, 10 Years of Juno, and Rubin Studies of TNOs
  • Press Conference: Studies of Rocky Body Atmospheres, the OSIRIS-Rex Mission, Connections to Exoplanets, and Characterization of the Outer Solar System
  • 2026 DPS Masursky Award: Saving NASA Science (Casey Dreier and Jack Kiraly)
  • 2026 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Characterizing Exoplanet Climates from Close-In Gas Giants to Temperate Rocky Planets (Tad Komacek)
  • 2026 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Unlocking Planetary Histories Through Subsurface Stratigraphies (Ali Bramson)
  • 2026 DPS Alexander Prize: Titan: Ingredients for Life (Catherine Neish)
  • 2026 DPS Kuiper Prize: New Worlds — Legacy Processes (Mark Marley)

Press Conference: Studies of Titan, Rocky Body Surfaces, 10 Years of Juno, and Rubin Studies of TNOs (Briefing video)

Devin Hoover (University of Arizona) described a study of Lyman-α (121.6 nm) emission from Titan. Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, is the only moon in the solar system with a significant atmosphere. Within Titan’s atmosphere, photochemistry creates a thick layer of haze and splits apart methane molecules, liberating hydrogen atoms that can escape to space. By monitoring the Lyman-α emission from this escaping hydrogen, researchers can study depletion of the methane in Titan’s atmosphere.

The calculated methane escape rate as a function of time. Click to enlarge. [From slide by Devin Hoover]

Titan’s Lyman-α emission was recorded by the Cassini mission, but many of those observations haven’t been analyzed. Hoover used a new radiative transfer model to interpret the Lyman-α emission, considering contributions from light scattered by hydrogen atoms as well as a direct contribution from interplanetary hydrogen. The team found hydrogen escape rates of order 1024–1025 hydrogen atoms per second, which is roughly consistent with theory and previous calculations. They also calculated methane escape rates, finding that the methane escape rate is highly sporadic and can be as rapid as 107–109 molecules cm-2 s-1. This is significantly faster than predicted by theory, and Hoover’s team has proposed that when lighter species like hydrogen escape from Titan’s atmosphere, they drag methane along with it, boosting its escape rate. If this explanation is correct, it would have important implications for the study of planetary atmospheres in general.

C. Adeene Denton (Southwest Research Institute) discussed new work on the creation of our Moon. In the canonical scenario, a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia crashed into the proto-Earth, forming a debris disk around the proto-Earth, and the Moon coalesced out of the debris disk. Modeling of this scenario typically uses smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations, which approximate the colliding bodies as fluids. This means that the bodies will deform like fluids do as they interact, and in the Moon-formation scenario, this leads Theia to be fully destroyed in the impact, creating a melt-dominated debris disk. The Moon is then built back up out of this debris disk in days to years.

Comparison of Moon-forming impact outcomes under different temperatures. Click to enlarge. [Slide by C. Adeene Denton]

Now, computational capabilities have increased, and modeled materials can have material strength — the ability of a material to resist deformation. Denton’s team found that incorporating material strength changes the outcome of the modeling: Theia splits into two pieces, one of which remains intact and becomes the Moon, resulting in nearly immediate Moon formation without a debris disk. The modeled newborn Moon is comparable in mass and rock/iron ratio to the present-day Moon. This scenario has interesting implications for age-dating the formation of the Moon, since the material strength of the protoplanets involved depends on their temperature and thus their age. Earlier in solar system history, when the protoplanets were hotter, it’s possible to obtain intact satellites, while later in history, when things are cooler, the surviving satellites are smaller. Future modeling may help to identify detectable differences between these scenarios.

Gokce Inal (Ohio State University) examined the impact of another recent technological advance: AI. Inal’s research was motivated by two questions: 1) Can AI understand the lunar surface the way a planetary scientist does? 2) Can AI make recommendations like a mission planner would? Inal’s team developed LLaVA-Le, an AI agent that can answer questions about orbital images of the Moon’s surface the way a scientist would. Then, a second AI agent called LUMINA can act as a mission planner, developing a ranked list of landing sites based on public NASA maps and landing rules. LUMINA created a list of 30 potential landing sites within a 72,000 km2 region at the Moon’s south pole, and all seven of NASA’s candidate lunar landing regions are in the AI’s top 16 regions.

Overview of LUMINA’s decision-making process for lunar landing site selection. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Gokce Inal]

LUMINA developed its recommendations based on a broad-to-narrow process that started with slope maps before screening based on temperature, sunlight, elevation, minerals, and other factors. The advantages of this technique for mission planning are that 1) each site is accompanied by the evidence underlying its selection, 2) it’s fast and easy to redo the site selection when a requirement or map changes, and 3) every spot on the map is checked, resulting in an analysis of 6,000 regions within 5 degrees of the south pole.

A diagram showing how Juno’s orbit will evolve over time, allowing the spacecraft to explore new regions. At the time of this writing, Juno recently completed its 88th close approach to Jupiter. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Scott Bolton]

NASA’s Juno mission has now been orbiting Jupiter for a little more than 10 years. Juno Principal Investigator Scott Bolton (Southwest Research Institute) described some of its key findings and how the mission has evolved over time. Juno is the first solar-powered mission to travel to Jupiter, and it monitors our solar system’s largest planet with a suite of 11 instruments and 30 sensors. Over time, Juno’s orbit has shifted, and the mission has been able to gain new perspectives on Jupiter’s atmosphere and pass close to several of its moons.

Early discoveries from the Juno mission include the finding that the atmosphere is not well mixed, and that the planet’s core, rather than being small and metal rich, is large, diluted, and depleted of heavy elements. Together, these findings suggest that sending a probe into the atmospheres of each of our solar system’s giant planets is unlikely to illuminate solar system history as once hoped. (So far, only Jupiter has been probed in this manner.) Juno also revealed Jupiter’s polar cyclones in vivid detail, showing that they have warm cores just like Earth’s tropical cyclones. Juno’s observations were also critical for constraining the thickness of the ice shells on several moons and demonstrating that while Io does not harbor a massive subsurface magma ocean, it likely has small, separate seas of magma. Now, as the mission continues, Juno will explore new regions and undertake new science.

Illustration of the location of the Neptune trojans within Neptune’s orbit. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Megan Schwamb]

The NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory is just getting started, and already the discoveries are starting to roll in. Megan Schwamb (Queen’s University Belfast) announced the discovery of several Neptune trojans with Rubin. The Neptune trojans are small, icy bodies that occupy Neptune’s orbit, leading and trailing the planet by 60 degrees. Trojans are important probes for the history of the solar system, and they play a crucial role in testing models of solar system evolution involving migration of the giant planets.

Neptune and Jupiter host the majority of the trojans in our solar system. So far, we’ve discovered about 16,000 Jupiter trojans and just 32 Neptune trojans — but researchers suspect that there are actually 4–10 times more Neptune trojans than Jupiter trojans. Nearly all of the known Neptune trojans inhabit the swarm that leads Neptune in its orbit, while just two occupy the trailing swarm. It’s not yet known whether these clouds of objects are actually symmetrical because the trailing cloud has been projected against the crowded plane of the Milky Way for 15 years. Now, Rubin has already discovered three trailing Neptune trojans (two confirmed and one candidate). By monitoring these objects and determining their colors, Rubin has also shown that the leading and trailing clouds of Neptune trojans have similar compositions. This is just the beginning: Rubin’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time will discover tens to hundreds of new Neptune trojans.

Return to Table of Contents.

Press Conference: Studies of Rocky Body Atmospheres, the OSIRIS-REx Mission, Connections to Exoplanets, and Characterization of the Outer Solar System (Briefing video)

Edward (Beau) Bierhaus (Lockheed Martin) reported on a serendipitous experiment enabled by the OSIRIS-REx mission to the asteroid Bennu. OSIRIS-REx touched down on Bennu, a 500-meter-wide rubble pile near-Earth asteroid, and collected a sample to return to Earth. This process required the lander to fire its thrusters and lift off from the surface of the asteroid, unintentionally carrying out an experiment relevant for planetary defense.

The thruster plume footprints and the erosion of the surface are correlated. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Edward Bierhaus]

Some near-Earth asteroids are potentially hazardous, and it’s not yet known how these objects respond to outside forces, which limits our ability to respond in a planetary defense scenario. (The Double Asteroid Redirection Test mission purposefully slammed a small spacecraft into an asteroid to test one approach to changing the course of an oncoming asteroid.) Bierhaus and collaborators modeled the effects of the thrusters on the surface of Bennu, showing that the footprints of the thruster plumes correlate with the erosion seen on the surface. OSIRIS-REx’s thrusters displaced more than 17 cubic meters of material, moving an estimated 16,000 kg of rubble. This also revealed that Bennu’s surface had a more complex structure than expected. Overall, this experiment showed that thrusters can move a lot of material on small bodies, offering a new way to probe the surface of these bodies without touching down — an experiment that OSIRIS-APEX will soon carry out on the asteroid Apophis.

Steven Desch (Arizona State University) described a search for the answer to a question posed 17 years ago: why is the Sun more depleted in refractory materials than 82% of solar twins? Early on, it was thought that this mystery could be solved by the presence of our solar system’s giant planets: perhaps our star is depleted in refractory materials (materials that remain solid up to relatively high temperatures) because these materials are locked away inside the giant planets. Further research disproved this theory, and now, Desch’s team has a new hypothesis: astronomers’ favorite scapegoat — magnetic fields — are to blame.

Desch and collaborators found that most stars are depleted in refractory materials relative to the clouds they formed in. This suggests that the Sun was born closer to the galactic center than commonly thought. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Steven Desch]

If the ratio of mass and magnetic flux in a molecular cloud is below a certain value, the magnetic field can slow the cloud’s collapse. This slowdown is especially effective on small, electrically charged dust grains, while larger dust grains are unaffected. This means that if magnetic fields are present, stars accrete less dust — a reservoir for refractory materials — and likely form with lower metallicity than their parent molecular clouds. Taking the effects of magnetic fields into account, Desch’s team found a range of refractory material depletions that aligned well with what is seen for solar twins, as well as a value for the Sun that matches observations. If the Sun is less metal rich than the cloud it came from, that would mean that the Sun could have been born much closer to the galactic center. If stars don’t match the metallicity of their parent molecular clouds, that would have huge implications, and this finding has not yet been incorporated into models of star formation.

Diagram of the infrared excess caused by a close-in debris disk around a white dwarf. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Jordan Steckloff]

Jordan Steckloff (Planetary Science Institute) discussed a conundrum regarding the formation of debris disks around white dwarfs. When a star like the Sun reaches the end of its main-sequence lifetime, it evolves into a red giant and eventually leaves behind its exposed stellar core in the form of a white dwarf. A white dwarf should radiate as a blackbody, but observations show that many white dwarfs have more infrared emission than expected. These infrared excesses are often interpreted as evidence for close-in disks of debris. Because a star’s transition to a red giant and then a white dwarf should destroy any close-in objects, these disks must form from material that has migrated inward during the star’s red giant phase.

Steckloff considered how the strength of these materials affects the size of the debris that forms during migration, finding that the characteristic size is in the range of 100–1,000 meters — much larger than the pulverized dust thought to inhabit a white dwarf’s debris disk. While the mystery of how a white dwarf’s dusty disk comes to be remains unsolved for now, future work that explores the impact of collisions or rotational disruption may hold clues.

Elizabeth Silber (Sandia National Laboratories) brought the discussion back to the OSIRIS-REx mission, describing what was learned from the journey of its sample return capsule through Earth’s atmosphere. Silber’s team is interested in what happens when objects slam into Earth’s atmosphere. These impacts generate shockwaves and low-frequency sound called infrasound. By monitoring the infrasound from an atmospheric impact, scientists hope to use models to extract the properties of the impacting object. However, it can be extremely difficult to determine how large the impacting object was and how much energy it deposited in our atmosphere, and it’s hard to know anything about the object itself without discovering an associated meteorite.

Map of sensors deployed along the reentry path of the OSIRIS-REx sample return capsule. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Elizabeth Silber]

By studying an object with known properties — the sample return capsule — the team was able to test their models of shockwave physics. Since the trajectory of the capsule was known in advance, they deployed 39 infrasound detectors along its path and compared the measured signal against the predictions of multiple shockwave models. They will apply what they learned from this study to situations where they don’t know the properties of the impacting object, helping to characterize incoming objects and predict their effects on Earth’s atmosphere.

Return to Table of Contents.

2026 DPS Masursky Award: Saving NASA Science, Casey Dreier and Jack Kiraly (The Planetary Society)

The 2026 Harold Masursky Award for Meritorious Service to Planetary Science was awarded to Casey Dreier and Jack Kiraly of the Planetary Society for “exceptional service to planetary science and space exploration.” Dreier described the Save NASA Science advocacy campaign, which worked to prevent a devastating 47% cut to NASA funding proposed in the fiscal year 2026 President’s Budget Request. This campaign unfolded on multiple levels, from highly successful social media posts (reaching 9 million views on Instagram reels about planetary science policy) to the re-establishment of the Congressional Planetary Science Caucus. Part of the campaign was the largest Day of Action for space science in history, bringing more than 300 advocates to Washington, DC. Dreier highlighted the year-round advocacy efforts of the Planetary Society, including the creation of a dashboard to track the scientific impact of NASA missions. These collective actions were successful, and Congress overwhelmingly rejected the proposed cuts.

Kiraly expanded on the year-round advocacy efforts of the Planetary Society and described upcoming opportunities. In January, there will be 90 or more new members of Congress, which may be a record. This presents an incredible opportunity to define the issue of planetary science funding for more than a fifth of the new Congress. The Planetary Society aims to reach these new members with the next Save NASA Science Day of Action, which will take place 31 January and 1 February 2027 in DC. Kiraly hopes that they can break last year’s record for participation and ward off another existential threat to space science. Check out the Save NASA Science Action Hub to learn more and get involved!

Return to Table of Contents.

2026 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Characterizing Exoplanet Climates from Close-In Gas Giants to Temperate Rocky Planets, Tad Komacek (Oxford University)

Tad Komacek was awarded a 2026 Harold C. Urey Prize in Planetary Science for “pioneering research in planetary science, which has fundamentally advanced our understanding of planetary atmospheres within the solar system and beyond.” In this presentation, Komacek discussed his work on characterizing exoplanet atmospheres, specifically of hot Jupiters and temperate rocky planets around M dwarfs.

Hot Jupiters are completely unlike anything we have in our solar system. These planets are close to their stars, tidally locked, strongly irradiated, and extremely hot, with equilibrium temperatures greater than 1000K. The irradiation gradient on these planets creates strong pressure gradients that drive intense winds. These rapid winds should bring things into equilibrium quickly, but observations show that hot Jupiters have day–night temperature differences of hundreds of degrees. Komacek showed that damping of gravity waves is responsible for maintaining this temperature difference.

Molecular hydrogen can dissociate in the atmospheres of ultra-hot Jupiters, changing their atmospheric dynamics. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Tad Komacek]

Hotter hot Jupiters have a larger temperature contrast, but this trend reverses at extremely high temperatures, in the rarefied realm of ultra-hot Jupiters, which have equilibrium temperatures >2200K. Above this temperature, molecular hydrogen dissociates, and the energy absorbed by dissociation (and released by recombination elsewhere in the atmosphere) changes these planets’ atmospheric dynamics, leading to a counterintuitive reduction of the day–night temperature gradient.

Komacek has also used models to explore mineral clouds on hot Jupiters. Using WASP-43b as an example, he showed that certain planets’ phase curves can’t be matched by cloudless models. Further work on observations of WASP-43b from JWST has suggested that this planet only has clouds on its nightside, prompting a need for models that couple clouds, circulation, and radiation.

Comparison of temperature and cloud cover on Earth and a temperate planet around an M dwarf. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Tad Komacek]

Turning to temperate planets around M dwarfs, Komacek showed that though these planets might be rocky like Earth, there’s no reason for them to be truly Earth-like. Because these planets are slowly rotating, they have large day–night temperature gradients — like hot Jupiters — rather than equator–pole temperature gradients like Earth. Many of these planets have lots of clouds on their daysides, softening spectral features and making their atmospheres difficult to study, with the faintest spectral features on planets with rotation periods longer than 10 days.

Komacek also described modeling work from a member of his research group who has estimated the thermal emission from M-dwarf exoplanets that are not transiting. This showed that the thermal emission, including certain spectral features, could be detectable for some planets by upcoming missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Return to Table of Contents.

2026 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Unlocking Planetary Histories Through Subsurface Stratigraphies, Ali Bramson (Purdue University)

Ali Bramson was awarded a 2026 Harold C. Urey Prize in Planetary Science for “her groundbreaking contributions to planetary science.” In a delightful extension of her childhood fascination with columnar basalts and the planetary history they convey, Bramson now explores planetary history through stratigraphy: the study of rock and other layers

Aerial view of ice layers in Mars’s polar ice cap. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Ali Bramson]

On Mars, Bramson has examined the ice layers making up the polar caps, where aerial images show layers in the exposed ice. Radar observations offer a different perspective, allowing researchers to probe even deeper. Radar data has shown that Mars’s north and south polar ice caps are fundamentally different from one another, though each ice cap shares similarities with the small, ice-filled craters that dot the surface around them. At the north pole, the ice cap and surrounding craters are similar deep down, but show some differences in the top 5 meters, suggesting that their lower layers of ice were placed concurrently or under similar environmental conditions, while modern-day ice is being shaped by the local environment. At the south pole, some craters look similar to the ice cap, while others do not. This suggests that these ice deposits formed under two different sets of environmental conditions.

Terraced craters in Arcadia Planitia. [Slide by Ali Bramson]

Moving away from the poles, visible ice becomes scarce, but you need only scratch the surface to find it. This was demonstrated by the Phoenix lander in 2008, when its robotic arm unearthed (unmarsed?) a swath of ice just a few centimeters below the surface. This discovery occurred around 68 degrees north, and ice — if present — is likely concealed under a much thicker layer of material at lower latitudes. Luckily, radar can reveal this ice as well. Bramson’s team examined a curious set of craters in Arcadia Planitia with a terraced appearance: evidence for subsurface layers. Using these craters, they determined that a subsurface ice sheet tens of meters thick and covering 1.2 million square kilometers resides under Arcadia Planitia. Recent impacts that expose this ice supports this assessment.

To close out the Mars portion of the talk, Bramson emphasized that studying ice on Mars is critical for constraining the planet’s climate; understanding its habitability, especially in terms of its water budget; and enabling future human explanation. She concluded with a brief detour to the Moon, where her team works to understand the extent of a different buried material: ancient lava flows that created the dark areas on the Moon’s surface. Using radar, Bramson’s team has shown that the buried lava flows are three times more extensive than thought, which important for our understanding of the Moon’s past volcanism.

Return to Table of Contents.

2026 DPS Alexander Prize: Titan: Ingredients for Life, Catherine Neish (University of Western Ontario and the Planetary Science Institute)

Catherine Neish was awarded the 2026 Claudia J. Alexander Prize in Planetary Sciences for “her scientific, leadership, and collaborative contributions to planetary science.” Neish’s topic was Titan, the only moon in our solar system with a dense atmosphere, and an intriguingly Earth-like one at that. Titan’s thick atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, and reactions between nitrogen, methane, and incoming photons create a smoggy blend of organic compounds.

Our understanding of Titan’s atmosphere and surface has evolved dramatically since 1944, when Gerard Kuiper discovered the moon’s atmosphere and saw that it contained methane. When Voyager 1 paid a visit in 1980, it found that the atmosphere was rich in nitrogen, expanding our understanding of Titan’s atmospheric chemistry, but the spacecraft carried no instruments capable of peering through the atmosphere to the surface. Finally, starting in 2004, the Cassini–Huygens mission revealed Titan as a strangely Earth-like world, with sand dunes, bright plains, lakes, and a young, weathered surface relatively unmarked by impact craters.

Thanks to Voyager and Cassini, Neish said, we now know that Titan has all the ingredients needed for life: an energy source (mainly the Sun), the necessary elements (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen), and a solvent. Titan actually has two plausible solvents: liquid methane and water. Liquid methane likely makes a poor solvent for the chemical reactions necessary for life, and any life that relies on methane would be so different from life as we know it that we might not even know what to look for. Water, on the other hand, we know to be a great solvent — but on Titan it’s frozen hard as rock.

Amino acids produced by mixing lab-grown Titan haze particle analogs with water. The two amino acids that are grayed out contain sulfur, which makes them unlikely to form on Titan. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Catherine Neish]

Titan’s water can liquefy briefly after an impact, potentially allowing the chemical reactions necessary for life to happen in the pool of impact melt. As a graduate student, Neish studied this possibility by exposing lab-grown Titan haze particles to liquid water. Reporting on her results as part of a program on the Discovery Channel in 2008, she showed that multiple amino acids found in life on Earth formed in this mixture in hours to days — likely fast enough to form on Titan before the impact melt refreezes. (In this program, she also cheerfully informed the audience that it would take a surprisingly long time to freeze to death in Titan’s 95K chill, so suffocation is probably how you’d go!)

Energized by this finding, Neish was excited for a mission to Titan that could search for evidence of amino acid formation. But when the results of the decadal survey rolled out in 2011, a Titan mission didn’t make the list. After pivoting to work on impact melt of the Moon, Neish got a call from a colleague inviting her to work on a proposal for a new Titan mission. That mission — Dragonfly — is now scheduled for launch in 2028, with arrival at Titan in the mid-2030s. Dragonfly will touch down between dunes near Selk crater, a young impact crater near Titan’s equator, offering an opportunity to study a region where organic materials and liquid water might have mixed in the past.

Return to Table of Contents.

2026 DPS Kuiper Prize: New Worlds — Legacy Processes, Mark Marley (University of Arizona)

Mark Marley was awarded the 2026 Gerard P. Kuiper Prize in Planetary Sciences for “outstanding contributions to the field of planetary science.” Marley centered this talk on processes that have been discovered and understood within the solar system, then extended to exoplanets and brown dwarfs, helping to place the planets in our solar system within the broader context of substellar worlds.

Marley focused on three processes: disequilibrium chemistry, clouds, and temperature inversions. Taking Jupiter as an example, Marley recounted the discovery of carbon monoxide in Jupiter’s atmosphere — a molecule that, under equilibrium chemistry, shouldn’t have been there. Researchers discovered that carbon monoxide was present because the mixing timescale on Jupiter was faster than the chemical equilibrium timescale, allowing carbon monoxide to be brought up high in the atmosphere.

Looking at this same process in brown dwarfs, Marley introduced Gliese 229B, the first unequivocal brown dwarf to be discovered. Gliese 229B is warmer than Jupiter but still quite cool, and it too has carbon monoxide in its atmosphere despite equilibrium chemistry saying it shouldn’t be there. Looking at a larger sample of brown dwarfs, researchers have mapped the presence of carbon monoxide as a function of effective temperature, using this relationship to understand how fast the atmospheres of these worlds are mixing as a function of temperature. This revealed changes in the depth of the convective boundary with temperature.

Observed space density of brown dwarfs as a function of effective temperature. There is a visible pileup of brown dwarfs at 1300K. [From slide by Mark Marley]

Moving to the second topic, Marley discussed some of the efforts to model clouds on brown dwarfs. Researchers have found that cloudy models are necessary to match observations for brown dwarfs with temperatures above about 1400K. At 1300K and below, cloudless models start to match better. Across just 100K, something is going on with clouds in brown dwarf atmospheres, but what? The answer appears to involve the interaction between global atmospheric dynamics and the clouds, producing holes in the clouds similar to those seen on Jupiter. This transition appears to have an impact on how brown dwarfs cool over time, causing a pileup of brown dwarfs with temperatures around 1300K.

Marley briefly touched on the final topic by noting that brown dwarfs appear to have temperature inversions (a localized reversal of the trend of decreasing atmospheric temperature with increasing altitude), but without nearby stars to heat their upper atmospheres, it’s not clear why. A student of Marley’s is working to understand the source of brown dwarfs’ temperature inversions.

Marley concluded by reemphasizing that many processes have been discovered and explored in planetary atmospheres before being applied to exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. Because of this connection between planetary science and substellar astrophysics, there are ample opportunities for human connections as well, bringing together planetary scientists and astronomers to advance our understanding of distant worlds.

Return to Table of Contents.

item.title: Direct Evidence for Outflow Driven by Wolf–Rayet Stars in the Nearby Galaxy PGC 44685
item.dc:creator: Kerry Hensley
item.description:
Qian Huang et al 2026 ApJ 1006 167 Observations of a nearby dwarf galaxy suggest that Wolf–Rayet stars are able to shape their environments on subkiloparsec scales, but their winds are not able to drive galaxy-scale outflows.

Observations of a nearby dwarf galaxy suggest that Wolf–Rayet stars are able to shape their environments on subkiloparsec scales, but their winds are not able to drive galaxy-scale outflows.

The post Direct Evidence for Outflow Driven by Wolf–Rayet Stars in the Nearby Galaxy PGC 44685 appeared first on AAS Nova.

item.title: DPS 58: Days 1 and 2
item.dc:creator: Kerry Hensley
item.description:
News from the 58th meeting of the AAS Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS): discovering a new dwarf planet candidate in our solar system, cracking mysteries about Europa's ice shell, clarifying our understanding of Titan's hazy dunes, and much more.

The post DPS 58: Days 1 and 2 appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: Today and Friday of this week, we’ll be posting summaries of selected sessions from the 58th Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS) meeting in Spokane, WA. The usual posting schedule for AAS Nova will resume on 2 November.

Table of Contents:

  • Press Conference: Twenty Years of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Studies of Ocean Worlds, and Interstellar Objects
  • 2025 Masursky Award Presentation: Io’s Lava Lakes: From Galileo to Juno (Rosaly Lopes)
  • 2025 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Physical Properties of Planetary Organics: From Titan Hazes to Protoplanetary Disks (Xinting Yu)
  • 2025 Urey Prize Presentation: Geophysical Adventures Across the Solar System (An Illustrated Story) (James Keane)
  • 2025 Alexander Prize Presentation: Everything Is Connected, So Small Things Matter (Matthew Hedman)
  • The DPS Planetary Science Workforce Surveys: Past Results and Future Plans (Julie Rathbun)
  • Press Conference: Studies of Interstellar Objects, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and the DPS Workforce Survey

Press Conference: Twenty Years of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Studies of Ocean Worlds, and Interstellar Objects (Briefing video)

An avalanche on Mars captured by HiRISE on MRO. [NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona]

Leslie Tamppari (NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory) kicked off the first press conference of DPS 58 with an overview of some of the many accomplishments of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), which is celebrating 20 years at Mars this year. MRO is currently in its seventh extended mission, and the orbiter continues to make progress on its main areas of exploration: surface and climate change throughout history, ice and volcanics, modern geological processes, and atmospheric climate and weather. The orbiter has advanced our understanding of these areas through its scientific instruments: the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) has revealed dynamic surface features such as active sand dunes, recurring slope lineae (narrow dark streaks that change seasonally), avalanches, and gullies; the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars mapped the mineralogy of Mars and has revealed the history of its water; the Context Camera has observed thousands of fresh craters, some of which are filled with ice; the Shallow Radar sounder experiment has probed beneath Mars’s surface, especially in icy polar regions; the Mars Color Imager has made daily global maps of the planet and has helped to track water-ice clouds and dust storms; and the Mars Climate Sounder has revealed climatological features in Mars’s atmosphere and helped to establish active periods for the planet’s dust storms.

An example of Europa’s chaos terrain from the Galileo spacecraft. [NASA/JPL]

Alyssa Rhoden (Southwest Research Institute) reported on findings related to Europa’s ice shell. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has a rocky core surrounded by a global liquid ocean, which is topped with an ice shell that is estimated to be anywhere from 3 to 30 km thick. The thickness of the ice shell is important because it controls the transport of material from the ocean to the surface and determines the cycling of energy necessary for life. Microwave radiometer thermal emission measurements from the Juno spacecraft suggest that the ice shell is 29 km thick in a particular region, but the thickness of the shell likely isn’t uniform across the entire moon. Rhoden combined models with the local ice-thickness estimate from Juno to create a global map of Europa’s ice shell thickness, which showed that the thickness varies from 21 to 31 km (or 18 to 36 km, if using a variable heat flux), with the thinnest regions found at middle latitudes. The team discovered that the thinnest areas overlap with Europa’s jumbled “chaos” terrain, which goes against predictions that the chaos regions would be found where the ice shell is thickest.

Fraction of ejected planetesimals for different giant planet architectures. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Leila Honarbakhsh]

Leila Honarbakhsh (Tulane University) explored how the formation of giant planets can impact the ejection of planetesimals into interstellar space. Honarbakhsh used models to understand how the growth of giant planets would affect a population of 70,000 synthetic planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — distributed throughout the solar system. The simulations followed the giant planets of our solar system as they proceeded through different phases of accretion, progressing from initial slow accretion to runaway accretion. The models showed that the architecture of the giant planets in a planetary system impacts how many planetestimals are ejected from the system. With only Jupiter present, 86% of planetesimals with initial orbital distances between 4 and 6 au are ejected. When Saturn was added to the simulations, the percentage of ejected planetesimals around the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn remained high, while adding Uranus and Neptune into the mix decreased the ejection efficiency around the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn, and relatively few planetesimals were ejected from around the orbits of Uranus and Neptune.

SPHEREx observations of 3I/ATLAS in August and December 2025. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Carey Lisse]

The final two presenters described research relating to 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object known to have entered our solar system. First, Carey Lisse (Johns Hopkins University) presented observations of 3I/ATLAS from SPHEREx — an all-sky mapping satellite that launched in March 2025 — and the XMM-Newton X-ray observatory. SPHEREx showed that 3I/ATLAS changed dramatically between August 2025 and December 2025; in August, it would have been reasonable to assume that 3I/ATLAS was a “nearly dead” comet that had already offgassed the majority of its volatile material, but by December, the comet more closely resembled a “newborn” comet making its first close approach to a star. These dramatically different behaviors can be reconciled if 3I/ATLAS was encased in a thick shell of material that was heavily processed by cosmic rays during the comet’s interstellar journey. As 3I/ATLAS approached the Sun, outgassing removed enough of this surface material to reach the pristine ice below. XMM-Newton collected the first X-ray spectrophotometric data of an interstellar comet, showing remarkable similarities between this ancient denizen of a distant planetary system and comets from our own backyard.

Isotopic abundances of 3I/ATLAS compared to selected solar system comets. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Martin Cordiner]

Finally, Martin Cordiner (NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; Catholic University of America) described JWST’s observations of 3I/ATLAS, which were made in August 2025, December 2025, and April 2026. These observations showed that 3I/ATLAS has extremely high isotopic abundance ratios (e.g., 12C/13C) and an extremely high deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio compared to solar system comets. These ratios imply that 3I/ATLAS formed in an exceedingly cold and low-metallicity region. Cordiner noted that it’s not possible to find such low metallicity in our galaxy today, though similar conditions must have been present around the time of the comet’s birth, 10–12 billion years ago. Thus, interstellar objects like 3I/ATLAS can give us insight into the chemical history of our galaxy. Right about now, JWST will be taking one last look at 3I/ATLAS as it continues its journey out of the solar system, and the telescope will search for final signs of outgassing from the comet, which is currently 12–13 au from the Sun.

Return to Table of Contents.

2025 Masursky Award Presentation: Io’s Lava Lakes: From Galileo to Juno, Rosaly Lopes (NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory)

An example of a lava lake on Earth, in Halema‘uma‘u, a pit crater in the Kīlauea caldera in Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park. [USGS]

Rosaly Lopes was awarded the 2025 Harold Masursky Award for Meritorious Service to Planetary Science for “deep and broad dedication to the advancement and health of planetary science in countless ways that extend beyond her duties as a JPL scientist.” In this plenary lecture, Lopes presented on the lava lakes that dot the surface of Io, Jupiter’s innermost moon. Lava lakes are large molten lava pools that are connected to a subsurface magma chamber. These features tend to remain active for a long time, and those on Earth show a variety of behaviors, including boiling and crusting over.

Voyager 1 image of Loki Patera on Io. [NASA/JPL/USGS]

When Voyager 1 snapped the first photos of the lava lake Loki Patera on Io, scientists didn’t immediately recognize it for what it was, as lava lakes are rare on Earth. Loki Patera is the largest patera (a broad, shallow, irregularly shaped crater, often created through volcanism) in the solar system at 200 kilometers across, and it produces 10% of the total thermal emission from Io. Later, the Galileo mission provided more clues to the nature of Io’s paterae. During close flybys, Galileo revealed that paterae on Io tend to be crusted over and have hot edges, which is similar to lava lakes on Earth. Curiously, some paterae feature cold islands, the source of which is still unknown.

Most recently, the Juno mission has provided the best view yet of these volcanic features. Though Juno wasn’t initially even supposed to look at Io, changes in orbit led the spacecraft to undertake close flybys of the moon. The Juno observations featured fine spatial resolution and revealed hot rings in 40 features across Io. The annular width of these rings is 3–30 meters, and the thickness of the crust is about 5–10 meters, with the crust likely being a few years old. Unlike lava lakes on Earth, the crust in Io’s paterae tends to be intact, without any fissures. Loki Patera remains mysterious, with no hot ring and two resurfacing waves.

Return to Table of Contents.

2025 DPS Urey Prize Presentation: Physical Properties of Planetary Organics: From Titan Hazes to Protoplanetary Disks, Xinting Yu (The University of Texas at San Antonio)

Xinting Yu was awarded a 2025 Harold C. Urey Prize in Planetary Science for “broad and impactful work in both planetary and exoplanet science, on both planetary surfaces and atmospheres.” Yu’s presentation introduced laboratory work dedicated to understanding the surface and atmosphere of Titan, Saturn’s largest moon.

Titan is seemingly Earth-like, with its thick, nitrogen-dominated atmosphere, its lakes and river channels, and its shifting dunes. However, what appears to be Earth-like is still quite alien: Titan’s atmosphere is yellow and hazy; its lakes and rivers are filled with liquid methane, not water; and its dunes are piled high with organic material rather than silicate sand.

Photograph of laboratory-created Titan haze particles. [Slide by Xinting Yu]

Yu described experiments using a wind tunnel to understand how sediment transport impacts Titan’s dunes. These experiments used crushed walnut shells and instant coffee grounds as a stand-in for the particles that make up Titan’s dunes. However, though these materials are appropriately organic and grainy, they aren’t a good analog for Titan’s dunes, which are likely made up of haze particles that have drifted down from the atmosphere. To make the wind tunnel experiments more relevant to Titan, Yu measured the material properties of laboratory-created haze particles called tholins. This revealed that the material that makes up Titan’s dunes is stickier and weaker than Earth sand and experiences little tribocharging (developing an electrical charge after rubbing together). This means that it’s likely difficult to transport Titan dune particles large distances, and transporting them any distance requires higher wind speeds than expected.

Polymer chains forming between particles. [Slide by Xinting Yu]

It’s not yet clear how haze particles turn into dune particles. Haze particles are only a few microns across, but the “sand” that makes up the dunes is made up of particles hundreds to thousands of microns across. Yu hypothesized that haze particles fall into Titan’s lakes and rivers, where they clump together to form larger particles. Yu’s team tested this hypothesis by soaking tholins in liquid hexane, which generated 50–100-micron aggregates. When the team added a stir bar to simulate turbulence, the particles formed huge clumps, reaching millimeter sizes, and showed signs of creating polymer chains.

Yu has constructed a laboratory apparatus called the Planetary Material CHaractErization Facility (PMCHEF), allowing the team to study the properties of Titan surface materials in a water-free and oxygen-free environment; the team’s work has shown that exposure to the water and oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere can affect the properties of these materials. Going forward, Yu will continue to study not just Titan, but other bodies inside and outside our solar system as well.

Return to Table of Contents.

2025 Urey Prize Presentation: Geophysical Adventures Across the Solar System (An Illustrated Story), James Keane (NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory)

Illustration of two possible models for Io’s interior. Click to enlarge. [James Keane]

James Keane was awarded a 2025 Urey Prize for “his broad and impactful research portfolio studying the geophysics of worlds across the solar system, including the Moon, Io, Arrokoth, Pluto, and Enceladus.” In this plenary, Keane described his work on the Moon and Io while presenting some of his geological illustrations. Keane’s drawing started as a way to stay alert during lectures, but it soon evolved into an opportunity to connect with the broader community.

The Moon and Io are roughly the same size and are both rocky, and though they have vastly different geography, they have both been shaped by volcanism and tidal heating, either currently or in the past. Many of the questions surrounding Io concern how tidal heating is dissipated within its interior. Central to this question is whether Io has a global magma ocean beneath its surface, which Juno has helped to answer. Io is flexed by Jupiter’s gravitational field as it orbits, and it physically changes shape. The amount of flexing depends on the structure of the moon — a global subsurface magma ocean would mean more flexing than a solid interior. Juno didn’t see the strong signal expected if Io has a global magma ocean, but other possibilities, such as a thin layer or scattered pockets of magma are still feasible.

Possible models for Io’s interior. [James Keane]

Keane then turned the discussion toward the largest and oldest impact basin on the Moon, the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin. The basin was likely created early in Earth’s history, placing the event older than the oldest Earth rock samples, the Apollo lunar rock samples, or the Perseverance Mars rover samples. The Artemis Moon mission is planned to touch down at the Moon’s south pole, on the edge of SPA but not within the basin itself. Because SPA is so geologically diverse, no one site allows us to address all possible science questions about this region. A proposed long-range sample-collecting rover called Endurance would undertake a trek of 2,000 kilometers — 50 times farther than a rover has driven on any other solar system body — to help answer this diverse set of questions.

Return to Table of Contents.

2025 Alexander Prize Presentation: Everything Is Connected, So Small Things Matter, Matthew Hedman (University of Idaho)

Matthew Hedman was awarded the 2025 Claudia J. Alexander Prize in Planetary Sciences for “his scientific, leadership, and collaborative contributions to planetary science.” Hedman began by describing how scientists study small pieces of a broad, complex, interconnected system, and if you go deep enough, you eventually encounter connections between seemingly disparate areas.

An example of spiral density waves in Saturn’s rings (the dense grouping of lines seen on the left side of the image). [NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute]

To illustrate this point, Hedman gave two examples of unexpected connections. First came the study of spiral density waves in Saturn’s rings. Many of these waves are known to be due to mean motion resonances with Saturn’s moons, but some of them can’t possibly be produced by moons. In the 1990s, researchers proposed that some of the density waves could be due to asymmetries and oscillations within Saturn, but it wasn’t until the Cassini mission that these predictions were confirmed. However, there were still some waves that weren’t predicted, which may provide evidence that Saturn has a “fuzzy” core in which hydrogen and helium are blended together with heavy elements.

The location of the μ ring of Uranus (left) and a comparison of the ring’s location and the orbits of certain moons (right). Click to enlarge. [Slide by Matthew Hedman]

The second, more speculative example involved Uranus’s mysterious μ ring. The μ ring is a faint outer ring made of tiny water ice particles, and unlike nearly all other tenuous rings in the solar system, it’s blue. The only other exception to this rule is Saturn’s E ring, which is produced by cryovolcanism on Saturn’s moon Enceladus. Uranus’s μ ring appears to be produced by the tiny moon Mab — could Mab also be a source of cryovolcanism? Not likely, Hedman says, as the moon spans just 12 km, precluding the possibility of a vast subsurface ocean to act as a cryovolcanic reservoir.

Instead, Hedman posited a potential connection with other blue inhabitants of our solar system: centaurs. Centaurs are small bodies that temporarily (for a few million years) inhabit orbits between Jupiter and Neptune. Some centaurs display comet-like activity, shedding dust that can be blue in color. Could Mab, then, be a centaur showing a very low level of activity? And if so, why is this the only moon of Uranus that is active, even though other moons of similar size and composition are not? And what is the connection between Mab and its neighboring moon Miranda? These questions remain unanswered for now, waiting for future connections to be made.

Return to Table of Contents.

The DPS Planetary Science Workforce Surveys: Past Results and Future Plans, Julie Rathbun (Cornell University)

Julie Rathbun spoke about the ongoing planetary science workforce survey. This is the third survey of planetary science workers, with the first two taking place in 2011 and 2020. The survey, which is being carried out by the statistics team at the American Institute of Physics, is suitable for everyone from students to retirees, and it aims to understand the size and demographics of the planetary science workforce.

A slide showing some of the results from the 2020 workforce survey. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Julie Rathbun]

Rathbun briefly shared some results from the 2011 and 2020 surveys:

  • members of the LGBTQ+ community are less likely to be involved with planetary science missions
  • universities are the largest employer of planetary scientists
  • NASA provides the majority of funding for planetary scientists
  • the planetary science workforce is getting more diverse, but it lags behind the overall US labor force, the STEM workforce, and the physical sciences workforce
  • DPS membership is also growing more diverse but still lags behind the field

If you’re a DPS member, you should have received an email inviting you to complete the survey — please fill it out and contribute to this important data-collection effort!

Return to Table of Contents.

Press Conference: Studies of Interstellar Objects, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and the DPS Workforce Survey (Briefing video)

First up was Darryl Seligman (Michigan State University) speaking on what we can learn from studying interstellar objects. Interstellar objects can help to illuminate parts of the planet formation process that we don’t yet understand, but that we know must be ubiquitous throughout the galaxy. During planet formation, objects are ejected from the system, and we’ve spotted three of these cast-out objects when they’ve entered our solar system. The composition of these interstellar interlopers can tell us something about where in their planetary systems they formed; objects forming near the water snow line — the location within a protoplanetary disk at which the temperature becomes low enough for water to freeze — are enriched in water, while objects forming near other molecules’ snow lines are enriched in those species. Seligman led the initial investigation into comet 3I/ATLAS, the latest interstellar visitor to our solar system, and his research team found that its composition suggests formation in the coldest regions of its planetary system, where cold giant planets would be necessary to eject it. After the discovery of 3I/ATLAS, Seligman was part of a team that spotted the comet in pre-discovery observations from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. This discovery suggests that many more interstellar objects could be hiding in survey data, potentially escaping notice because they are moving quickly across the sky.

Modeling of 3I/ATLAS’s spectrum. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Silvia Protopapa]

Silvia Protopapa (Southwest Research Institute) described JWST observations of 3I/ATLAS’s coma. The spectrum of 3I/ATLAS’s coma is different from those of comae of solar system comets; while 3I/ATLAS and solar system comets both have a strong absorption feature around 3 microns, solar system comets have two additional absorption features at 1.5 and 2.0 microns that 3I/ATLAS’s spectrum lacks. Protopapa modeled spectra of ice grains, starting with grains of pure water ice, which shows all three spectral features seen in solar system comets. As the modeled ice grains were made increasingly dusty, the two shorter-wavelength features faded away, leaving a spectrum very similar to that of 3I/ATLAS. While 3I/ATLAS’s spectrum is different from the typical solar system comet, it’s similar to the average Kuiper Belt object spectrum. This tells us that ice grains in a planetary system can be composed of pure water ice or be laden with dust, and that the purity or dustiness of ice in a planetary system may be determined early, during the protoplanetary disk phase.

Observations and estimated properties of three ultra-fast rotators. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Dmitrii Vavilov]

Dmitrii Vavilov (University of Washington) reported on the discovery of super-fast and ultra-fast rotators in early data from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Asteroids larger than roughly 200 meters across are believed to be gravitationally bound piles of rubble rather than single large rocks. This means that large asteroids can only rotate so fast before flying apart, but despite the hypothetical 2.2-hour limit to their rotation, large asteroids have now been found rotating as quickly as once every 2 minutes. Vavilov and collaborators discovered dozens of rapidly rotating asteroids (a few of which are classified as “ultra-fast rotators” with rotation periods of less than 5 minutes) in Rubin’s first-look and Data Preview 2 observations. Intriguingly, all of the fastest rotators are C-type asteroids, which are thought to be weaker than other types of asteroids. Based on the rotation speeds seen here, these asteroids must have material strengths close to that of solid rock.

Comparison of 2026 ED138 to confirmed dwarf planets in our solar system. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Matthew Holman]

Mario Juric (University of Washington) and Matthew Holman (Harvard University) presented on another discovery from Rubin Observatory: a new dwarf planet candidate in our solar system. Holman discovered the object, named 2026 ED138, just two weeks ago. 2026 ED138 has a diameter between 600 and 1,500 km and lies 47 au from Earth, journeying around the Sun once every 280 years. It’s among the brightest trans-Neptunian objects known, but it’s not yet clear if it’s a relatively small, reflective object or a relatively large, darker object. To verify the discovery, the researchers searched for the object in earlier data and found it in observations from the Dark Energy Camera from 10 years ago, among other places. Because the object is so bright — bright enough for capable amateur astronomers to spot it, let alone professional telescopes — it’s surprising that it evaded detection so long, but it managed to hide among crowded fields of stars in the plane of the Milky Way. Though 2026 ED138 is still a dwarf planet candidate at the moment, future infrared observations will help to pin down its size and may promote it to confirmed dwarf planet status. Hopefully, this is just one of many such discoveries that we can expect from Rubin!

Data from the 2020 planetary science workforce survey showing the varied backgrounds of planetary scientists. Click to enlarge. [Slide by Julie Rathbun]

Finally, Julie Rathbun (Cornell University) discussed some of the findings of the DPS workforce survey, which was also the topic of a plenary talk earlier in the day. The DPS is currently embarking on a new survey of the planetary science workforce, which aims to understand the humans behind the science and quantify the diversity in training, subfield, techniques, employment, and demographics among planetary scientists. Rathbun summarized two findings from previous surveys, which were conducted in 2011 and 2020: 1) planetary scientists are interdisciplinary, with training in numerous fields, and 2) planetary science is getting more diverse, but the diversity of planetary scientists lags behind that of the overall US labor force, the STEM workforce, and the physical science workforce.

Return to Table of Contents.

The post DPS 58: Days 1 and 2 appeared first on AAS Nova.

item.title: These “Ice Giants” Have a Hot Secret
item.dc:creator: Astrobites
item.description:
Astrobites reports on a possible piping-hot secret about the so-called "ice giant" planets in our solar system, Uranus and Neptune.

The post These “Ice Giants” Have a Hot Secret appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: Astrobites is a graduate-student-run organization that digests astrophysical literature for undergraduate students. As part of the partnership between the AAS and astrobites, we occasionally repost astrobites content here at AAS Nova. We hope you enjoy this post from astrobites; the original can be viewed at astrobites.org.

Title: Ice Giants Revisited: Uranus and Neptune as Magma Ocean Worlds
Authors: Edward D. Young et al.
First Author’s Institution: University of California, Los Angeles
Status: Published in ApJ

You’re probably used to seeing tabloids in the checkout aisle of the grocery store claiming all sorts of wild things. Perhaps it’s a celebrity couple who’s about to break up or have a baby. Maybe it’s an exposé on the fiery feud between movie co-stars who just can’t stand each other. It’s even more likely to be some terrible secret that the royal family is desperately trying to cover up. The scandals of life on Earth are abundant, and it seems like the rest of the solar system isn’t any different. Although you might not see their pictures on the front covers of any gossip magazines, Uranus and Neptune may not be what you think. These “ice giant” planets have a piping-hot secret that the authors of today’s article are exposing.

THE OLD STORY COMES OUT

Figure 1: The canonical three-layer model of an ice giant’s interior. The core is composed of silicate rocks. The mantle is made up of ices of water, methane, or ammonia. The atmosphere is dominated by hydrogen and helium, with trace amounts of methane. [Evan Nelles Henderson]

After our Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago, a disk of leftover gas and dust called a protoplanetary disk remained around it. In the inner, hotter part of the disk, elements like iron, silicon, and magnesium coalesced into the small dense rocky planets you know and love today: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. In the outer, colder part of the protoplanetary disk, where water freezes into solid grains of ice, larger planets formed. This includes the gas giants, Jupiter and Saturn, which were massive enough to undergo runaway gas accretion of hydrogen and helium, ballooning up to incredible masses, albeit with overall low densities. Further out still, we find Uranus and Neptune, which are known as “ice giants” due to their intermediate mass and density. Uranus and Neptune have previously been thought to be composed of a rocky core, a middle layer of ices, and an outer layer of hydrogen and helium with trace amounts of methane (Figure 1). But something about this story smells rotten, and it’s not just the methane…

AN ICY CONSPIRACY

Can we really trust what we think we know about the composition of Uranus and Neptune? They are the only two planets that went undetected by humankind until the invention of the telescope, so they have a history of being sneaky. The authors of today’s article note that the canonical three-layer model of an ice giant’s interior structure described above is not the only way to explain the known properties of these two planets. Firstly, their interiors may not be separated cleanly into three distinct compositions, since mixing can occur between the layers (Figure 2).

Figure 2: The interior structure of Uranus and Neptune proposed by today’s article. A well-mixed magma ocean with dissolved hydrogen sits at the bottom and a hydrogen dominated envelope is on top. In the middle is a transition zone where molten silicate rain falls back to the magma ocean. Click to enlarge. [Young et al. 2026]

Furthermore, several lines of evidence suggests that Uranus and Neptune may not even contain very much ice at all. So much for “ice giant”! The many asteroids and dwarf planets found in the Kuiper Belt, which are thought to be representative of the material from which Uranus and Neptune formed, are primarily composed of rock, not ice. Additionally, observations show that protoplanetary disks around faraway stars are also ice poor.

When we look to the planets of other stars, we see lots of sub-Neptune-size planets, but their interior structures remain an unsolved problem in astronomy, and it’s unclear whether sub-Neptune exoplanets are ice-poor gas dwarfs or ice-rich water worlds. We reached out to Uranus and Neptune for a comment, but they didn’t get back to us.

MAGMA HOT GOSSIP

So, if the “ice giants” might not be made of ice, what the Herschel are they made of? The authors of today’s article explore the possibility of Uranus of Neptune being better described as magma ocean worlds with overlying atmospheres dominated by hydrogen and helium. This possibility is supported by theoretical molecular dynamics simulations, which suggest that at high pressures, hydrogen gas can dissolve into magma, forming a well-mixed fluid. This mixing may explain Uranus and Neptune’s intermediate density, previously interpreted as ices. In this model, there is a transition zone at the surface of the magma ocean (called a binodal), where molten silicate rock separates from the hydrogen and rains back down into the magma ocean. Above the binodal, the composition becomes almost entirely hydrogen and helium with no remaining rocky material.

INSIDERS REVEAL

How well does this model match real-life observations? The authors check to see if their magma ocean model can reproduce six key properties of Uranus and Neptune, many of which were measured precisely by the Voyager 2 mission:

  • the radius corresponding to 1 bar of pressure
  • the temperature corresponding to 1 bar of pressure
  • the moment of inertia (how the planet’s mass is distributed from its centre)
  • the intrinsic luminosity (how much heat comes up from the planet’s interior)
  • and two gravitational harmonics correction terms (coming from the fact that the planets aren’t perfect spheres)

The authors use a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to predict the values of three parameters that simultaneously reproduce all six observed properties. Those three parameters are the following:

  • the total hydrogen mass fraction of the planet
  • the pressure at the transition zone from magma ocean to gas envelope
  • and the strength of convection in the gas envelope

This interior structure model (Figure 3) is simple in the sense that it only has three free parameters, but complex enough to capture important physical effects like the planets’ rotation and winds.

Figure 3: The best-fit models for Neptune and Uranus derived in the article, shown as a density map across planetary depth. The surface of the magma ocean is visible as a sudden drop in density at the boundary layer (sharp change from red to yellow). [Young et al. 2026]

THE SHOCKING TRUTH

Overall, this magma ocean model reproduces the observable properties of Uranus and Neptune well. The only exception is Neptune’s 1-bar temperature, which is overestimated, likely due to large uncertainties in the opacity assumed for the atmosphere. Additionally, this model of a magma ocean world provides elegant explanations for many of the unique features of Uranus and Neptune. For example, Uranus’s ultra-low intrinsic luminosity (basically no heat coming up from the interior) can be naturally explained by strong chemical gradients at the transition zone that suppresses heat flow due to convection. Also, the lack of ammonia observed in the atmospheres of both planets can be easily explained by the fact that ammonia dissolves readily into magma oceans, pulling it out of the atmosphere.

It should be noted that this is one of several models that can successfully describe the observed properties of Uranus and Neptune. This model does have its advantages, though, such as the fact that it has a small number of free parameters (only three), which makes it easier to test and less prone to overfitting. It also assumes that Uranus and Neptune are made of similar material to gas dwarf exoplanets, suggesting they’re scaled down versions of Jupiter and Saturn. How cute!

So next time you’re looking at the tabloids as you check out at the grocery store, consider the possibility of a magma ocean scandal on Uranus and Neptune. Planetary scientists can make shocking reveals too, just like the paparazzi.

Original astrobite edited by Elise Koo.

About the author, Evan Nelles Henderson:

I’m a master’s student at McMaster University in Hamilton, Canada. My areas of research include exoplanets, mantle–atmosphere coupling, and the origins of life. Outside of research, I enjoy board games, running, and house music.

The post These “Ice Giants” Have a Hot Secret appeared first on AAS Nova.

item.title: Seeing Red: New Constraints on Origin of JWST’s Little Red Dots
item.dc:creator: Alexia Kubas
item.description:
Supercritical accretion of black holes may drive the formation of enigmatic "little red dots."

The post Seeing Red: New Constraints on Origin of JWST’s Little Red Dots appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
NASA’s JWST has found a population of compact, red light sources called “little red dots” (LRDs). Numerous hypotheses have been proposed to explain these optical phenomena, and a new study further constrains their origin.

Schematic of the outflow model used by the team. Arrows denote the direction of flow. [Liu et al. 2026]

Under (Radiation) Pressure

“Little” red dots appear to be no more than a few hundred light-years across and have many hypothesized sources, from direct-collapse black holes to supermassive stars. A favored interpretation is that LRDs are gaseous envelopes housing massive black holes, but the formation mechanism of such an envelope has been unclear. A new study led by Jun-Rong Liu at the Chinese Academy of Sciences reveals that supercritical accretion of black holes may explain the origin of such envelopes.

Supercritical accretion occurs when a black hole accretes material at such an extreme rate that radiation pressure expels some of the material in an optically thick outflow. Such outflows are thought to create massive, glowing envelopes of material. The team modeled this process and compared simulated envelope properties to real observations of LRDs.

Luminosities and temperatures of real LRDs (blue circles) overlaying expected values from modeled envelopes (dotted and dashed lines). Most observations fall between 105 M⊙ < MBH < 107 M⊙ and 1,500 < ṁ < 5,000. [Liu et al. 2026]

Connecting the Dots

The team’s model of radiation-driven outflow depends on two key parameters: black hole mass (MBH) and accretion rate (ṁ). Accretion rate is a dimensionless value, and anything larger than 1 is classified as supercritical accretion. These variables dominate the physics of the model and affect the temperature, luminosity, and spectral features of the resulting envelope.

The team tested a range of black hole masses and accretion rates and compared their simulated envelope spectra against 36 real LRDs. The modeling suggested that black hole masses between 105 and 107 M⊙ and accretion rates between 1,500 and 5,000 are necessary to match the estimated temperatures and luminosities of LRDs. Supercritical, indeed!

Distributions of Balmer break strength (left) and Balmer decrement (right) in LRDs (blue) and expected values from the model assuming MBH = 106 M⊙ and ṁ = 2,000 (orange). Click to enlarge. [Adapted from Liu et al. 2026]

Reading Between the (Spectral) Lines

Liu and collaborators then tested whether simulated LRDs within this range of black hole masses and accretion rates could reproduce several characteristics of real LRD spectra: the strength of the Balmer break (a sharp decrease in spectral intensity at 3645 Angstroms that acts as a proxy for the density of the envelope), the Balmer decrement (the ratio between the Hα and Hβ emission), and the width of the source’s broad emission lines (which quantifies the velocity dispersion of the gaseous envelope as it circles the black hole within).

The team’s model produced a range of Balmer break strengths consistent with real LRDs. Modeled broad emission line widths (also known as full width at half maximum) were also a good match. The one area where the model diverged from observations was the Balmer decrement. Real LRDs exhibit Hα/Hβ ratios of ∼4–17, and the team’s models were in the 3–8 range, overlapping with the lower end of the observed distribution.

Overall, the team’s model of radiation-driven outflows from supercritical accretion of black holes produced envelopes with features broadly consistent with real observations of LRDs, providing a plausible origin of these little light sources.

Citation

“Optically Thick Outflow Driven by Supercritical Accretion May Explain Little Red Dots,” Jun-Rong Liu et al 2026 ApJL 1007 L13. doi:10.3847/2041-8213/ae8dba

The post Seeing Red: New Constraints on Origin of JWST’s Little Red Dots appeared first on AAS Nova.

item.title: Anybody Home? Black Hole Occupation Fraction Helps Clarify Galactic History
item.dc:creator: Lucas Brown
item.description:
Most galaxies are expected to contain at least one massive black hole, but how robust is this prediction? New research uses simulations to look at which galaxies tend to have more or fewer black holes, and with what properties.

The post Anybody Home? Black Hole Occupation Fraction Helps Clarify Galactic History appeared first on AAS Nova.
item.content:encoded:
Most galaxies are thought to contain at least one massive black hole, but how absolute is this association, really — and what can it tell us about galactic evolution?

Is There Anybody Home?

Massive black holes are everywhere. Well, not quite everywhere — but they are almost always found lurking deep within galaxies. The reason for this is somewhat straightforward: black holes can form in the early universe, and the repeated black hole mergers that occur as galaxies collide and grow over billions of years inevitably lead to some of these black holes ballooning to massive or supermassive status.

The ubiquity of massive black holes is quantified by the black hole occupation fraction (BHOF), a number that represents the fraction of all galaxies that contain at least one such object. For high-mass galaxies, determining the BHOF is relatively straightforward. In these systems, central black holes can have significant dynamical effects that enable direct detections, and observational evidence suggests that the BHOF is close to 1. When it comes to lower-mass galaxies, however, the BHOF is harder to measure. Black holes in lower-mass galaxies often cannot accrete enough material to form bright accretion disks or noticeably disrupt visible matter and stars, making it difficult to determine whether the BHOF stays close to unity across all galaxy masses. 

Galaxies are typically expected to contain at least one if not dozens of massive black holes (black and yellow circles). Their individual positions and electromagnetic signatures can vary greatly in different galaxies, however, as demonstrated by this simulated galaxy. [Ricarte et al. 2021]

Understanding the BHOF has implications for the study of galactic evolution. In high-mass galaxies, successive mergers and dense cores enable the formation of supermassive black holes — but also homogenize the central black holes, erasing clues to their origins. In low-mass galaxies, the position and masses of central black holes may retain some variation that can inform us about their origins. In the absence of robust observational data on the BHOF in low-mass galaxies, a team led by Emma Jane Weller (Yale University) decided to examine the next best thing: cosmological simulations.

Location, Location, Location!

Weller and collaborators utilized ASTRID, a high-resolution cosmological simulation that includes a sophisticated prescription for seeding and evolving black holes. Unlike in some other cosmological simulations, when massive black holes are formed they are not simply forced to sit at the centers of their host galaxies. Rather, perturbations from mergers and interactions with other black holes can displace them, creating two classes of massive black holes: central and wandering — where wandering black holes are any that sit in the outer half of their host galaxies. The simulation is also able to determine when a black hole undergoes significant accretion.

The total, central, and wandering BHOF (colored lines) for galaxies of various masses found in the ASTRID simulation. Recent constraints on the BHOF from Zou et al. 2025 are overlaid in gray. [Weller et al. 2026]

By examining the BHOF across a variety of systems, the authors identified a few notable trends. While the total BHOF remained very close to 1 across the entire mass range, the types of black holes varied significantly. For low-mass galaxies, the central BHOF fell over time, while the wandering BHOF rose. This trade-off can be explained by repeated mergers displacing central black holes. In small galaxies, shallow gravitational potentials make it difficult for these black holes to return to galactic centers after a merger. These off-center systems rarely accrete and are generally difficult to observe. This result has important implications for observational studies, because without understanding the prevalence of wandering black holes, observations of galaxies without an obvious black hole could be wrongly interpreted as evidence for inefficiency in the black hole seeding process.

Weller and collaborators additionally found that the BHOF for strongly accreting black holes was much smaller than the total BHOF, especially after cosmic noon where galactic growth slows. As with the trends in wandering versus central black holes, this finding highlights the need for nuanced interpretations of observational constraints on the BHOF, as the location, activity, and overall observability of massive black holes can vary significantly depending on their galactic environment, merger history, and age.

Citation

“The Black Hole Occupation Fraction as a Fossil Record of Seeding, Dynamics, and Galaxy Assembly,” Emma Jane Weller et al 2026 ApJL 1008 L54. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ae9c38

The post Anybody Home? Black Hole Occupation Fraction Helps Clarify Galactic History appeared first on AAS Nova.

Galaxy Assembly,” Emma Jane Weller et al 2026
